name: Banana
shortDescription: A fast-ripening fruit that changes quickly from green to spotted brown.
storageMethod: Keep bananas at room temperature away from direct sunlight. Once ripe, they can be moved to the refrigerator to slow further ripening, although the peel will darken.

shelfLife.roomTemperature: About 3–5 days once ripe (green bananas need a few extra days to ripen)
shelfLife.refrigerator: About 3–4 extra days once ripe (the peel darkens, but the fruit inside usually stays fine)
shelfLife.freezer: Peeled: about 3 months for best quality

storageTips: Separate bananas from the bunch to slow ripening slightly.
Keep them away from other fruit if you want to avoid speeding up ripening.
Peel and freeze overripe bananas in pieces for smoothies or baking.

freshnessStages.label: Underripe
freshnessStages.description: Green or very firm. Needs a few days at room temperature.

freshnessStages.label: Ripe
freshnessStages.description: Yellow and firm-soft. Sweet and easy to peel.

freshnessStages.label: Use Soon
freshnessStages.description: Brown spots and softer texture. Great for smoothies and baking.

freshnessStages.label: Check Quality
freshnessStages.description: Very dark, leaking or mushy. Look closely for mold or a sour smell.

freshnessSigns: Yellow peel with a few small spots
spoilageSigns: Visible mold on the peel or the flesh
Leaking liquid or very slimy texture

name: Apple
shortDescription: A crisp fruit that stores well when kept cool.
storageMethod: Apples keep their crispness longest in the refrigerator, ideally in the crisper drawer. At room temperature they soften faster.

shelfLife.refrigerator: About 4 weeks in the crisper drawer
shelfLife.freezer: Sliced or cooked: about 8 months for best quality (texture becomes soft)

storageTips: Store apples away from strongly scented foods.
Keep bruised apples separate so they do not affect the others.
Wash just before eating rather than before storing.

freshnessStages.label: Fresh
freshnessStages.description: Firm, crisp and smooth-skinned.

freshnessStages.label: Softening
freshnessStages.description: Slightly soft or wrinkled. Better cooked than eaten raw.

freshnessStages.label: Use Soon
freshnessStages.description: Soft spots or bruises. Cut away small bruises or bake.

freshnessStages.label: Check Quality
freshnessStages.description: Mushy, leaking or moldy. Inspect carefully.

spoilageSigns: Large soft, brown or leaking areas

name: Strawberry
shortDescription: A delicate berry that softens and molds quickly.
storageMethod: Store unwashed strawberries in the refrigerator in a breathable container lined with paper towel. Wash only just before eating.

shelfLife.refrigerator: About 3–5 days
shelfLife.freezer: Washed, dried and hulled: about 10 months for best quality (texture becomes soft)

storageTips: Remove any soft or moldy berries right away so mold does not spread.
Do not wash until you are ready to eat them.
Freeze extra berries on a tray first, then move them to a bag.

freshnessStages.label: Fresh
freshnessStages.description: Bright red, firm, with green leaves.

freshnessStages.label: Use Soon
freshnessStages.description: Slightly soft or darker. Good for smoothies or jam.

freshnessStages.label: Check Quality
freshnessStages.description: Mushy, leaking or with fuzzy patches. Check carefully for mold.

name: Tomato
shortDescription: Best ripened on the counter, then used within a few days.
storageMethod: Keep unripe tomatoes at room temperature out of direct sun until they ripen. Ripe tomatoes can go in the refrigerator if you cannot use them in time; bring them to room temperature before eating for better flavour.
shelfLifePreview: Room temp: about 2–3 days once ripe

shelfLife.roomTemperature: Ripe: about 2–3 days. Unripe: about 3–5 days to ripen first
shelfLife.refrigerator: About 5 days once ripe (flavour and texture may dull)
shelfLife.freezer: Best for cooking: about 2 months (texture becomes soft)

storageTips: Store stem-side down to reduce bruising.
Do not stack tomatoes; they bruise easily.
Freeze soft tomatoes and use them in sauces or soups.

freshnessStages.label: Ripening
freshnessStages.description: Firm and still pale. Leave at room temperature.

freshnessStages.label: Ripe
freshnessStages.description: Deep colour, slight give and a tomato smell.

freshnessStages.label: Use Soon
freshnessStages.description: Soft and wrinkly skin. Good for sauces and soups.

freshnessStages.label: Check Quality
freshnessStages.description: Leaking, collapsing or moldy. Inspect carefully.

name: Potato
shortDescription: A hardy vegetable that lasts weeks in a cool, dark place.
storageMethod: Store potatoes in a cool, dark, well-ventilated place. Avoid sunlight, which can turn them green. Do not keep them next to onions.

shelfLife.pantry: About 3–4 weeks in a cool, dark, ventilated place
shelfLife.freezer: Only after cooking or blanching: about 3 months (raw potatoes freeze poorly)

storageTips: Keep potatoes in a paper bag or basket, not sealed plastic.
Remove any spoiled potato so the others stay in good condition.
Avoid washing until you are ready to cook.

freshnessStages.label: Fresh
freshnessStages.description: Firm, smooth skin with no sprouts.

freshnessStages.label: Use Soon
freshnessStages.description: Small sprouts or slight softening. Use soon and remove sprouts.

freshnessStages.label: Check Quality
freshnessStages.description: Green patches, heavy sprouting, shriveling or softness. When in doubt, avoid.

name: Spinach
shortDescription: Tender leafy greens that wilt quickly if stored damp.
storageMethod: Keep spinach in the refrigerator in a container lined with paper towel to absorb moisture. Wash just before using.

shelfLife.refrigerator: About 5 days (bagged spinach: follow the product label)
shelfLife.freezer: Blanched: about 10 months for best quality (texture becomes soft)

storageTips: Moisture speeds up spoilage, so keep leaves dry.
Remove any slimy leaves as soon as you see them.
Wilted but otherwise fresh spinach is best cooked.

freshnessStages.label: Fresh
freshnessStages.description: Crisp, bright green leaves.

freshnessStages.label: Use Soon
freshnessStages.description: Slightly wilted. Best cooked in soup or stir-fries.

freshnessStages.label: Check Quality
freshnessStages.description: Slimy, yellowing or smelly. Avoid if in doubt.

name: Milk
shortDescription: A cold-chain dairy staple that should be kept refrigerated.
storageMethod: Store milk in the main body of the refrigerator (not the door) and keep the container closed. Do not leave it out for long periods.

shelfLife.refrigerator: About 5–7 days after opening; unopened milk: use by the label date
shelfLife.freezer: About 3 months (leave space in the container; texture may separate)

storageTips: Return milk to the refrigerator right after pouring.
Never pour used milk back into the container.
Check the product label and storage instructions on the pack.

freshnessStages.label: Fresh
freshnessStages.description: Cold, sealed or recently opened, with a mild smell.

freshnessStages.label: Use Soon
freshnessStages.description: Nearing the label date or opened for several days.

freshnessStages.label: Check Quality
freshnessStages.description: Sour smell, lumps or unusual look. Do not consume if in doubt.

name: Yogurt
shortDescription: A cultured dairy food that keeps well when cold.
storageMethod: Keep yogurt tightly covered in the refrigerator. Use a clean spoon each time to avoid introducing contamination.

shelfLife.refrigerator: About 5–7 days after opening; unopened: use by the label date
shelfLife.freezer: About 2 months (texture becomes grainy or watery)

storageTips: Keep the lid on tightly after each use.
A little watery liquid on top can be normal; stir it in and check smell and appearance.
Do not leave yogurt out of the refrigerator for long periods.

freshnessStages.label: Fresh
freshnessStages.description: Smooth, creamy and pleasantly tangy.

freshnessStages.label: Use Soon
freshnessStages.description: Nearing the label date or opened for several days.

freshnessStages.label: Check Quality
freshnessStages.description: Mold, strong sour smell or unusual look. Avoid if in doubt.

name: Cheese
shortDescription: Shelf life depends a lot on type, from soft cheeses to hard blocks.
storageMethod: Wrap cheese in wax paper or parchment, then place it in a loose container in the refrigerator. Do not wrap it too tightly in plastic for long periods.

shelfLife.refrigerator: Hard cheese: about 3–4 weeks after opening. Soft cheese: about 1–2 weeks after opening
shelfLife.freezer: About 2 months for best quality (texture becomes crumbly)

storageTips: Wrap each type of cheese separately.
Use clean utensils to cut cheese.
For soft cheese with mold, follow food-safety guidance or avoid it.

freshnessStages.label: Fresh
freshnessStages.description: Normal colour, smell and texture for its type.

freshnessStages.label: Use Soon
freshnessStages.description: Dry edges, sweating or opened for a while.

freshnessStages.label: Check Quality
freshnessStages.description: Mold, slime or sharp off smell. Avoid soft cheese with mold; check guidance for hard cheese.

spoilageSigns: Visible mold, especially on soft cheese

name: Bread
shortDescription: Goes stale within days, but the freezer extends its life.
storageMethod: Keep bread in a breadbox or sealed bag at room temperature. Freeze slices if you will not finish the loaf within a few days.

shelfLife.roomTemperature: About 4–5 days for packaged sliced bread; bakery loaves are best within 2–3 days
shelfLife.freezer: About 3 months for best quality

storageTips: The refrigerator can dry bread out faster, so room temperature or freezer is usually better.
Slice before freezing so you can take out only what you need.
Stale bread is a quality issue, not necessarily a safety issue, and is good for toast or breadcrumbs.

freshnessStages.label: Fresh
freshnessStages.description: Soft with a pleasant smell.

freshnessStages.label: Use Soon
freshnessStages.description: Getting dry or stale. Good for toast, croutons or breadcrumbs.

freshnessStages.label: Check Quality
freshnessStages.description: Any visible mold or a musty smell. Avoid the whole loaf.

spoilageSigns: Green, white or black mold spots

name: Rice
shortDescription: Dry rice keeps for a long time; cooked rice needs quick, careful storage.
storageMethod: Keep dry rice in an airtight container in a cool, dry pantry. For cooked rice, cool it quickly, store it in the refrigerator, and reheat until steaming hot.
shelfLifePreview: Dry: about 1 year · Cooked: 3–4 days in fridge

shelfLife.pantry: Dry white rice: about 1 year for best quality. Brown rice: about 6 months
shelfLife.refrigerator: Cooked rice: about 3–4 days in a sealed container
shelfLife.freezer: Cooked rice: about 1 month for best quality

storageTips: Do not leave cooked rice at room temperature for long; refrigerate it within about 1–2 hours.
Store dry rice away from moisture and pests.
Reheat cooked rice until steaming hot and do it only once.

freshnessStages.label: Dry: Stable
freshnessStages.description: Uncooked rice kept dry and sealed stays good for a long time.

freshnessStages.label: Cooked: Fresh
freshnessStages.description: Just cooked, cooled quickly and stored in the refrigerator.

freshnessStages.label: Cooked: Use Soon
freshnessStages.description: Second or third day in the refrigerator. Use in fried rice.

freshnessStages.label: Check Quality
freshnessStages.description: Slimy, hard or smelly rice. Avoid if in doubt.

freshnessSigns: Dry rice: no moisture or clumping
Cooked rice: fluffy and neutral smell
spoilageSigns: Damp clumps, mold or insects in dry rice

name: Pasta
shortDescription: Dry pasta is a long-lasting pantry staple; cooked pasta is short-lived.
storageMethod: Keep dry pasta in a sealed container in a cool, dry pantry. Refrigerate cooked pasta in an airtight container within about 2 hours.
shelfLifePreview: Dry: about 2 years · Cooked: 3–4 days in fridge

shelfLife.pantry: Dry pasta: about 2 years for best quality
shelfLife.refrigerator: Cooked pasta: about 3–4 days in a sealed container
shelfLife.freezer: Cooked pasta: about 2 months for best quality

storageTips: Store dry pasta away from moisture and pests.
Toss cooked pasta with a little oil before storing to prevent sticking.
Reheat cooked pasta until steaming hot.

freshnessStages.label: Dry: Stable
freshnessStages.description: Uncooked pasta stays good for a long time when kept dry.

freshnessStages.label: Cooked: Fresh
freshnessStages.description: Freshly cooked or newly refrigerated.

freshnessStages.label: Cooked: Use Soon
freshnessStages.description: Several days in the refrigerator. Use in a bake or stir-fry.

freshnessStages.label: Check Quality
freshnessStages.description: Slimy texture, smell or mold. Avoid if in doubt.

freshnessSigns: Cooked pasta: firm and neutral smell
spoilageSigns: Moisture, mold or insects in dry pasta

name: Mango
shortDescription: A summer favourite that ripens on the counter and softens fast once ready.
storageMethod: Ripen firm mangoes at room temperature, out of direct sun. Once a mango gives slightly when pressed and smells sweet at the stem, move it to the refrigerator to slow it down.

shelfLife.roomTemperature: About 2–5 days for a firm mango to ripen
shelfLife.refrigerator: Ripe and whole: about 5 days. Cut: about 3 days in a sealed container
shelfLife.freezer: Peeled cubes: about 6 months for best quality

storageTips: Judge ripeness by feel and smell, not colour: some varieties stay green when ripe.
Do not refrigerate unripe mangoes; cold stops them ripening properly.
Freeze very ripe mango in cubes for smoothies or lassi.

freshnessStages.label: Unripe
freshnessStages.description: Hard, little smell. Leave it at room temperature for a few days.

freshnessStages.label: Ripe
freshnessStages.description: Gives slightly when pressed, sweet smell at the stem end.

freshnessStages.label: Use Soon
freshnessStages.description: Very soft with some wrinkling or dark patches on the skin.

freshnessStages.label: Check Quality
freshnessStages.description: Leaking, fermented smell or mould near the stem. Avoid if in doubt.

freshnessSigns: Sweet, fruity smell at the stem
spoilageSigns: Mould near the stem or on soft spots
Mushy, stringy flesh with dark streaks

name: Papaya
shortDescription: A soft tropical fruit that turns from green to yellow-orange as it ripens.
storageMethod: Ripen papaya at room temperature until the skin is mostly yellow and gives slightly when pressed. Keep ripe papaya whole in the refrigerator, and store cut pieces in a sealed container.

shelfLife.roomTemperature: About 2–4 days for a part-yellow papaya to ripen
shelfLife.refrigerator: Ripe and whole: about 1 week. Cut: about 2–3 days
shelfLife.freezer: Peeled chunks: about 6 months for best quality

storageTips: A fully green papaya may never ripen well; choose one with some yellow.
Scoop out the seeds before storing cut papaya.
Cover cut surfaces so the flesh does not dry out or pick up fridge smells.

freshnessStages.label: Unripe
freshnessStages.description: Mostly green and firm. Leave it at room temperature.

freshnessStages.label: Ripe
freshnessStages.description: Yellow-orange skin, slight give, sweet smell.

freshnessStages.label: Use Soon
freshnessStages.description: Soft spots and a few dark marks. Eat it today.

freshnessStages.label: Check Quality
freshnessStages.description: Sunken, leaking or mouldy areas. Avoid if in doubt.

name: Guava
shortDescription: A fragrant fruit that goes from crisp to soft in just a few days.
storageMethod: Keep firm guavas at room temperature until they soften slightly and smell fragrant. Move ripe guavas to the refrigerator and eat them within a few days.

shelfLife.roomTemperature: About 2–5 days, depending on how firm it was when bought
shelfLife.refrigerator: Ripe: about 3–4 days
shelfLife.freezer: Cut and deseeded: about 6 months for best quality

storageTips: Keep guavas apart from other fruit; they ripen quickly and give off a strong smell.
Eat crisp guavas with salt and chilli, or wait for soft ones if you prefer them sweet.
Check the base for small holes, which can mean fruit-fly damage.

freshnessStages.label: Crisp
freshnessStages.description: Green and firm. Good for eating with salt and chilli.

freshnessStages.label: Ripe
freshnessStages.description: Pale yellow-green, slight give, strong sweet smell.

freshnessStages.label: Use Soon
freshnessStages.description: Soft with brown patches. Best for juice or jam.

freshnessStages.label: Check Quality
freshnessStages.description: Mushy, leaking or mouldy. Avoid if in doubt.

spoilageSigns: Mould at the base or stem

name: Orange
shortDescription: A citrus fruit with a protective peel that keeps for weeks when cold.
storageMethod: Keep oranges loose in a cool place for up to a week, or in the refrigerator crisper to keep them much longer. Do not store them in a sealed plastic bag; trapped moisture causes mould.

shelfLife.refrigerator: About 3–4 weeks in the crisper drawer
shelfLife.freezer: Juice or segments: about 4–6 months for best quality

storageTips: Check the bag and remove any orange with mould so it does not spread.
Heavier oranges for their size are usually juicier.
Bring cold oranges to room temperature for the best flavour.

freshnessStages.label: Fresh
freshnessStages.description: Firm, heavy for its size, glossy peel.

freshnessStages.label: Ripe
freshnessStages.description: Fully coloured, fragrant, slightly softer.

freshnessStages.label: Use Soon
freshnessStages.description: Soft or dry spots, peel beginning to wrinkle. Juice it.

freshnessStages.label: Check Quality
freshnessStages.description: Blue-green or white mould, or a fermented smell. Avoid.

name: Lemon
shortDescription: Keeps for weeks in the fridge and is easy to use up a little at a time.
storageMethod: Store lemons in the refrigerator, ideally in a closed container or bag in the crisper, to stop them drying out. Wrap cut lemons and use them within a few days.

shelfLife.refrigerator: Whole: about 3–4 weeks. Cut: about 3–4 days
shelfLife.freezer: Juice in ice-cube trays: about 4 months for best quality

storageTips: Roll a lemon firmly on the counter before cutting to get more juice.
Zest lemons before juicing them and freeze the zest.
Hard, dry lemons still have usable zest even when the juice is gone.

freshnessStages.label: Fresh
freshnessStages.description: Firm, bright yellow, fragrant peel.

freshnessStages.label: Use Soon
freshnessStages.description: Softening, or hard and drying at the ends.

freshnessStages.label: Check Quality
freshnessStages.description: Mould on the peel, or mushy patches. Avoid if in doubt.

name: Grapes
shortDescription: Sweet bunches that keep best cold, dry and unwashed.
storageMethod: Keep grapes unwashed in the refrigerator in a ventilated bag or open container. Wash only the amount you are about to eat, and remove any soft or mouldy grapes first.

shelfLife.refrigerator: About 1–2 weeks, unwashed
shelfLife.freezer: Washed, dried and frozen whole: about 3 months for best quality

storageTips: Moisture causes mould, so dry grapes well if you do wash them.
Leave grapes on the stem until you eat them.
Frozen grapes make a simple cold snack.

freshnessStages.label: Fresh
freshnessStages.description: Plump, firm, attached to green, flexible stems.

freshnessStages.label: Use Soon
freshnessStages.description: Some grapes softening or wrinkling, stems browning.

freshnessStages.label: Check Quality
freshnessStages.description: Leaking, mouldy or fizzy-smelling grapes. Remove them.

freshnessSigns: A light natural bloom on the skin
spoilageSigns: Fuzzy grey mould where grapes touch

name: Pomegranate
shortDescription: A thick-skinned fruit that keeps well whole; the seeds spoil much faster.
storageMethod: Keep whole pomegranates in a cool place for a week or two, or in the refrigerator for much longer. Store the removed seeds (arils) in a sealed container in the refrigerator.

shelfLife.roomTemperature: Whole: about 1–2 weeks in a cool, dry place
shelfLife.refrigerator: Whole: about 1–2 months. Seeds: about 5 days
shelfLife.freezer: Seeds spread on a tray, then bagged: about 6 months for best quality

storageTips: Choose fruit that feels heavy for its size.
Remove the seeds in a bowl of water to avoid splashes.
Dry seeds well before refrigerating them.

freshnessStages.label: Fresh
freshnessStages.description: Heavy, firm, with tight, leathery skin.

freshnessStages.label: Use Soon
freshnessStages.description: Skin drying and hardening, a few soft spots.

freshnessStages.label: Check Quality
freshnessStages.description: Brown, mushy seeds or a sour smell inside. Avoid.

spoilageSigns: Mould at the crown or on cut seeds

name: Watermelon
shortDescription: Keeps for days whole, but cut melon needs the fridge.
storageMethod: Keep an uncut watermelon in a cool place out of the sun. Once cut, cover the flesh tightly or move pieces to a sealed container and refrigerate.

shelfLife.refrigerator: Whole: about 2 weeks. Cut: about 3–5 days
shelfLife.freezer: Cubes: about 6 months (soft once thawed, fine for drinks)

storageTips: Wash the rind before cutting so the knife does not carry dirt into the flesh.
Do not leave cut watermelon out in a warm room.
Blend soft pieces into juice rather than throwing them away.

freshnessStages.label: Fresh
freshnessStages.description: Heavy, firm rind with a creamy yellow ground spot.

freshnessStages.label: Cut: Fresh
freshnessStages.description: Crisp, juicy, bright red flesh.

freshnessStages.label: Use Soon
freshnessStages.description: Cut flesh turning watery or slightly mealy. Make juice.

freshnessStages.label: Check Quality
freshnessStages.description: Slimy flesh, sour smell or mould. Avoid.

name: Pineapple
shortDescription: Does not get sweeter after picking, so eat it while it smells fragrant.
storageMethod: Keep a whole pineapple at room temperature for a day or two, or refrigerate it to slow decline. Store cut pineapple in a sealed container in the refrigerator.

shelfLife.refrigerator: Whole: about 3–5 days. Cut: about 3–4 days
shelfLife.freezer: Chunks: about 6 months for best quality

storageTips: A sweet smell at the base is a better guide than colour.
Pineapple does not ripen further after harvest; it only softens.
Cut away and discard any brown, fermented-smelling flesh.

freshnessStages.label: Fresh
freshnessStages.description: Firm, fragrant at the base, green leaves.

freshnessStages.label: Use Soon
freshnessStages.description: Softer, darker skin, very sweet smell.

freshnessStages.label: Check Quality
freshnessStages.description: Leaking, mouldy base or vinegary smell. Avoid.

spoilageSigns: Mould at the base or on cut flesh

name: Pear
shortDescription: Ripens from the inside out, so check the neck rather than the body.
storageMethod: Ripen pears at room temperature. Check ripeness by pressing gently near the stem; when it gives, the pear is ready and can go in the refrigerator for a few days.

shelfLife.refrigerator: Ripe: about 3–5 days
shelfLife.freezer: Cooked or poached: about 10 months for best quality

storageTips: Pears ripen from the inside, so a firm body can hide a soft core.
Keep them out of sealed bags at room temperature.
Cut pears brown quickly; a squeeze of lemon helps.

freshnessStages.label: Unripe
freshnessStages.description: Hard all over. Leave it at room temperature.

freshnessStages.label: Ripe
freshnessStages.description: The neck gives slightly when pressed.

freshnessStages.label: Use Soon
freshnessStages.description: Soft and bruising. Poach or bake it.

freshnessStages.label: Check Quality
freshnessStages.description: Brown, mushy core or mould. Avoid if in doubt.

name: Kiwi
shortDescription: A fuzzy fruit that ripens on the counter and keeps for weeks once cold.
storageMethod: Ripen firm kiwis at room temperature until they give slightly, then keep them in the refrigerator. Unripe kiwis also keep for weeks in the refrigerator and can be ripened later.

shelfLife.roomTemperature: About 3–7 days for a firm kiwi to ripen
shelfLife.refrigerator: Ripe: about 1–2 weeks. Unripe: up to about 4 weeks
shelfLife.freezer: Peeled slices: about 6 months (soft once thawed)

storageTips: Kiwis ripen faster next to apples or bananas.
A ripe kiwi feels like a ripe peach: slight give, not soft.
Eat the skin of golden varieties if you like; it is thinner.

freshnessStages.label: Unripe
freshnessStages.description: Hard and sour. Ripen at room temperature.

freshnessStages.label: Ripe
freshnessStages.description: Gives slightly, sweet and juicy.

freshnessStages.label: Use Soon
freshnessStages.description: Soft and wrinkling. Use in a smoothie.

freshnessStages.label: Check Quality
freshnessStages.description: Mushy, leaking or mouldy. Avoid.

name: Avocado
shortDescription: Hard when bought, perfect for a day or two, then brown fast.
storageMethod: Ripen avocados at room temperature. When one yields to gentle pressure, eat it or move it to the refrigerator to hold it for a couple of days. Wrap a cut half with the stone left in.

shelfLife.refrigerator: Ripe: about 2–3 days. Cut half, wrapped: about 1 day
shelfLife.freezer: Mashed with lemon juice: about 4–6 months

storageTips: Flick off the stem cap: green underneath means ripe, brown means overripe.
Lemon or lime juice slows browning on cut flesh.
Overripe but not rotten avocado still works in smoothies or baking.

freshnessStages.label: Unripe
freshnessStages.description: Hard, often bright green. Leave it out for a few days.

freshnessStages.label: Ripe
freshnessStages.description: Yields to gentle pressure, green under the stem cap.

freshnessStages.label: Use Soon
freshnessStages.description: Soft, with some dark streaks inside. Mash it today.

freshnessStages.label: Check Quality
freshnessStages.description: Black flesh, sour smell or mould. Avoid.

spoilageSigns: Mould on the skin or flesh

name: Blueberries
shortDescription: Small berries that last longest dry, cold and unwashed.
storageMethod: Refrigerate blueberries unwashed in their ventilated box or an open container lined with paper towel. Pick out soft or mouldy berries, and wash only what you will eat.

shelfLife.refrigerator: About 5–10 days, unwashed
shelfLife.freezer: Spread on a tray, then bagged: about 10–12 months

storageTips: One mouldy berry can spread to the rest; check the box when you buy it.
The dusty white bloom is natural and protects the berry.
Freeze extras on a tray so they do not stick together.

freshnessStages.label: Fresh
freshnessStages.description: Firm, dusty-blue berries that roll freely.

freshnessStages.label: Use Soon
freshnessStages.description: Some berries soft or wrinkled. Bake or blend them.

freshnessStages.label: Check Quality
freshnessStages.description: Fuzzy mould, leaking juice or a sour smell. Remove them.

freshnessSigns: Dry box with no juice stains

name: Peach
shortDescription: A soft stone fruit that ripens on the counter and bruises at a touch.
storageMethod: Ripen firm peaches at room temperature, stem side down and not touching each other. Once a peach smells sweet and gives slightly near the stem, move it to the refrigerator and eat it within a few days.

shelfLife.roomTemperature: About 1–3 days for a firm peach to ripen
shelfLife.refrigerator: Ripe: about 3–5 days. Cut: about 1–2 days in a sealed container
shelfLife.freezer: Sliced: about 10–12 months for best quality

storageTips: Handle peaches gently; bruises turn brown and soft within a day.
Do not refrigerate unripe peaches; cold makes the flesh dry and mealy.
A paper bag speeds up ripening if you need them sooner.

freshnessStages.label: Unripe
freshnessStages.description: Hard, with a green tinge near the stem. Leave it out for a day or two.

freshnessStages.label: Ripe
freshnessStages.description: Sweet smell, slight give near the stem, golden background colour.

freshnessStages.label: Use Soon
freshnessStages.description: Very soft or bruised in places. Bake, blend or cook it today.

freshnessStages.label: Check Quality
freshnessStages.description: Leaking, wrinkled, fermented smell or mould. Avoid if in doubt.

name: Fig
shortDescription: Fresh figs are delicate and keep for only a few days, even when cold.
storageMethod: Keep ripe fresh figs in a single layer in the refrigerator, on a paper-lined plate or in a shallow container, and eat them within a couple of days. Wash just before eating.

shelfLife.refrigerator: About 2–3 days in a single layer
shelfLife.freezer: Whole or halved: about 6 months (soft once thawed, fine for cooking)

storageTips: Do not stack figs; their weight bruises the ones below.
Figs do not ripen much after picking, so choose soft, fragrant ones.
Dried figs are a different product and keep for months in the pantry.

freshnessStages.label: Fresh
freshnessStages.description: Plump and soft, with a sweet smell and an intact skin.

freshnessStages.label: Use Soon
freshnessStages.description: Very soft, starting to wrinkle or split. Eat or cook it today.

freshnessStages.label: Check Quality
freshnessStages.description: Sour or fermented smell, leaking or mould. Throw it out.

spoilageSigns: White or grey mould, often at the base

name: Onion
shortDescription: A dry-skinned bulb that keeps for weeks somewhere cool, dark and airy.
storageMethod: Store whole onions in a cool, dry, well-ventilated place such as a basket or mesh bag. Keep them away from potatoes, which make them spoil faster. Refrigerate cut onion in a sealed container.

shelfLife.pantry: Whole: about 1–2 months in a cool, dry, airy place
shelfLife.refrigerator: Cut or peeled: about 7–10 days in a sealed container
shelfLife.freezer: Chopped: about 8 months (for cooking only)

storageTips: Do not store onions in plastic bags; they need air.
Keep onions and potatoes apart.
Use sprouting onions soon; the green shoots can be eaten like spring onion.

freshnessStages.label: Fresh
freshnessStages.description: Firm, heavy, with dry papery skin.

freshnessStages.label: Use Soon
freshnessStages.description: Starting to sprout or slightly soft at the neck.

freshnessStages.label: Check Quality
freshnessStages.description: Soft, wet, black mould or a rotten smell. Avoid.

spoilageSigns: Black powdery mould under the skin

name: Garlic
shortDescription: Whole bulbs keep for months; peeled cloves need the fridge.
storageMethod: Keep whole garlic bulbs in a cool, dry, airy place out of direct light. Once a bulb is broken, use the cloves within about 10 days. Refrigerate peeled cloves in a sealed container.

shelfLife.pantry: Whole bulb: about 3–5 months. Separated cloves: about 10 days
shelfLife.refrigerator: Peeled cloves: about 1 week in a sealed container
shelfLife.freezer: Peeled or chopped: about 6 months

storageTips: Do not store raw garlic in oil at room temperature; it can grow dangerous bacteria.
Green sprouts in the centre are safe but can taste bitter; remove them.
Keep garlic in a mesh or paper bag, not plastic.

freshnessStages.label: Fresh
freshnessStages.description: Firm, tight bulb with dry papery skin.

freshnessStages.label: Use Soon
freshnessStages.description: Green sprouts appearing or cloves softening.

freshnessStages.label: Check Quality
freshnessStages.description: Soft, brown, hollow or mouldy cloves. Avoid.

name: Ginger
shortDescription: A knobbly root that keeps for weeks in the fridge if kept dry.
storageMethod: Store unpeeled ginger in a dry, sealed bag or container in the refrigerator crisper. Peel and grate only what you need. Freeze extra ginger and grate it straight from frozen.

shelfLife.refrigerator: Unpeeled: about 3–4 weeks. Peeled: about 2 weeks
shelfLife.freezer: Whole or grated: about 6 months

storageTips: Pat ginger dry before storing; moisture invites mould.
Scrape the skin off with a spoon to waste less.
Frozen ginger grates more easily than fresh.

freshnessStages.label: Fresh
freshnessStages.description: Firm, smooth skin, snaps cleanly.

freshnessStages.label: Use Soon
freshnessStages.description: Wrinkled skin and drier flesh. Still fine for cooking.

freshnessStages.label: Check Quality
freshnessStages.description: Soft, mouldy or dark inside. Avoid.

spoilageSigns: Mould on the skin or cut ends

name: Carrot
shortDescription: A sturdy root that stays crisp for weeks when cold and covered.
storageMethod: Cut off any leafy tops, then store carrots in a bag or covered container in the refrigerator crisper. The tops pull moisture out of the root if left on.

shelfLife.refrigerator: About 3–4 weeks with tops removed
shelfLife.freezer: Blanched: about 10–12 months

storageTips: Bendy carrots are not spoiled; soak them in cold water to crisp them up.
Keep carrots away from apples and bananas, which can make them bitter.
Peel only before using.

freshnessStages.label: Fresh
freshnessStages.description: Firm, bright orange, snaps cleanly.

freshnessStages.label: Use Soon
freshnessStages.description: Bendy or with small white hairs. Fine for cooking.

freshnessStages.label: Check Quality
freshnessStages.description: Slimy, mushy or mouldy. Avoid if in doubt.

name: Cucumber
shortDescription: Mostly water, so it softens quickly once it starts to go.
storageMethod: Keep cucumbers dry in the refrigerator, ideally wrapped in a cloth or paper towel inside a bag. Keep them away from tomatoes and bananas. Wrap cut ends tightly.

shelfLife.refrigerator: Whole: about 1 week. Cut: about 2–3 days

storageTips: Store them in the warmer front of the fridge; very cold spots damage them.
Wipe off moisture before storing.
Soft but not slimy cucumbers can still go into raita.

freshnessStages.label: Fresh
freshnessStages.description: Firm, dark green, crisp when cut.

freshnessStages.label: Use Soon
freshnessStages.description: Slightly soft at the ends or a little wrinkled.

freshnessStages.label: Check Quality
freshnessStages.description: Slimy, mushy or mouldy. Avoid.

name: Bell Pepper
shortDescription: Capsicum keeps a week or two in the fridge; green lasts longer than red.
storageMethod: Store whole, dry bell peppers in the refrigerator crisper. Keep cut peppers in a sealed container and use them within a few days.

shelfLife.refrigerator: Whole: about 1–2 weeks (green lasts longest). Cut: about 3–4 days
shelfLife.freezer: Sliced: about 10–12 months (for cooking only)

storageTips: Red, yellow and orange peppers are riper than green and spoil sooner.
Do not wash peppers until you are ready to use them.
Wrinkled peppers are still fine roasted or in curries.

freshnessStages.label: Fresh
freshnessStages.description: Firm, glossy and heavy for its size.

freshnessStages.label: Use Soon
freshnessStages.description: Wrinkling or slightly soft. Roast or cook it.

freshnessStages.label: Check Quality
freshnessStages.description: Slimy, sunken spots or mould. Avoid.

spoilageSigns: Mould near the stem or inside

name: Green Chilli
shortDescription: Lasts longer with the stems removed and kept dry.
storageMethod: Remove the stems, discard any soft chillies, then store them dry in a paper-lined container in the refrigerator. Freeze extras whole.

shelfLife.refrigerator: About 1–2 weeks, stems removed and kept dry
shelfLife.freezer: Whole: about 6 months

storageTips: Removing the stems slows rotting.
Keep them dry; damp chillies turn slimy.
Wash your hands after handling chillies.

freshnessStages.label: Fresh
freshnessStages.description: Firm, bright green and glossy.

freshnessStages.label: Use Soon
freshnessStages.description: Some turning red or wrinkling. Still fine to cook.

freshnessStages.label: Check Quality
freshnessStages.description: Black, slimy or mouldy chillies. Throw them out.

spoilageSigns: Black or dark brown soft spots

name: Cauliflower
shortDescription: Firm white curds that develop brown spots as they age.
storageMethod: Keep cauliflower unwashed in a loosely closed bag in the refrigerator, stem side up so moisture does not collect on the florets.

shelfLife.refrigerator: Whole: about 4–7 days. Florets: about 3–4 days
shelfLife.freezer: Blanched florets: about 10–12 months

storageTips: Small light-brown spots can be cut off; the rest is fine.
Wash only just before cooking.
The leaves and stem are edible: cook them with the florets.

freshnessStages.label: Fresh
freshnessStages.description: Tight, creamy-white head with green leaves.

freshnessStages.label: Use Soon
freshnessStages.description: Small brown spots appearing. Cut them off and cook.

freshnessStages.label: Check Quality
freshnessStages.description: Spreading dark spots, mushy or mouldy. Avoid.

name: Cabbage
shortDescription: A tight head of leaves that keeps for weeks whole and cold.
storageMethod: Keep cabbage whole in the refrigerator crisper with the outer leaves on. Wrap a cut head tightly and use it within a few days.

shelfLife.refrigerator: Whole: about 2 weeks, often longer with outer leaves on. Cut: about 3–4 days
shelfLife.freezer: Blanched: about 9 months (for cooking only)

storageTips: Peel off wilted outer leaves; the inside is usually still crisp.
Do not wash until you are ready to use it.
Shredded cabbage loses vitamins quickly; cut it close to cooking.

freshnessStages.label: Fresh
freshnessStages.description: Heavy, firm head with crisp, tight leaves.

freshnessStages.label: Use Soon
freshnessStages.description: Outer leaves wilting or yellowing. Remove them.

freshnessStages.label: Check Quality
freshnessStages.description: Slimy, dark or smelly leaves inside. Avoid.

name: Broccoli
shortDescription: Tight green florets that turn yellow within days of purchase.
storageMethod: Store broccoli unwashed in the refrigerator in a loosely closed bag or wrapped in a damp towel. Use it within a few days.

shelfLife.refrigerator: About 3–5 days
shelfLife.freezer: Blanched florets: about 10–12 months

storageTips: Yellow florets mean it is ageing: cook it soon.
Peel and slice the stem; it tastes like the florets.
Do not seal it airtight; it needs a little air.

freshnessStages.label: Fresh
freshnessStages.description: Deep green, tight florets, firm stem.

freshnessStages.label: Use Soon
freshnessStages.description: Some florets turning yellow. Cook it today.

freshnessStages.label: Check Quality
freshnessStages.description: Slimy, mouldy or strongly smelly. Avoid.

name: Okra
shortDescription: Bhindi bruises easily and goes slimy if stored damp.
storageMethod: Keep okra completely dry in a paper bag or paper-lined container in the refrigerator. Wash and dry it well only just before cooking.

shelfLife.refrigerator: About 2–3 days, dry
shelfLife.freezer: Blanched: about 10–12 months

storageTips: Moisture is the main enemy: never store okra wet.
Choose small, tender pods; large ones can be woody.
Dry okra completely after washing so it does not turn slimy in the pan.

freshnessStages.label: Fresh
freshnessStages.description: Bright green, firm, tip snaps cleanly.

freshnessStages.label: Use Soon
freshnessStages.description: Some dark marks or softening. Cook it today.

freshnessStages.label: Check Quality
freshnessStages.description: Slimy, black or mouldy pods. Throw them out.

name: Eggplant
shortDescription: Baingan bruises easily and turns bitter as it ages.
storageMethod: Keep eggplant whole and unwashed in the warmer part of the refrigerator, such as the crisper, and use it within a few days. Very cold spots can damage it.

shelfLife.refrigerator: About 4–5 days
shelfLife.freezer: Cooked or roasted: about 6–8 months

storageTips: Cut eggplant browns quickly; cook it soon after slicing.
A green, fresh-looking cap is a good sign.
Handle gently; bruises turn brown and soft.

freshnessStages.label: Fresh
freshnessStages.description: Glossy, firm skin that springs back when pressed.

freshnessStages.label: Use Soon
freshnessStages.description: Dull skin, slight wrinkling or soft spots.

freshnessStages.label: Check Quality
freshnessStages.description: Mushy, brown inside or mouldy. Avoid.

name: Mushroom
shortDescription: Button mushrooms sweat in plastic; give them a paper bag instead.
storageMethod: Store mushrooms unwashed in a paper bag or their original ventilated box in the refrigerator. Brush or wipe them clean just before cooking.

shelfLife.refrigerator: About 3–7 days in a paper bag
shelfLife.freezer: Sautéed: about 10–12 months

storageTips: Do not wash mushrooms before storing them.
Plastic traps moisture and makes them slimy.
Slightly wrinkled mushrooms are fine to cook.

freshnessStages.label: Fresh
freshnessStages.description: Firm, smooth, dry caps with closed gills.

freshnessStages.label: Use Soon
freshnessStages.description: Darkening, a little wrinkled or open gills. Cook today.

freshnessStages.label: Check Quality
freshnessStages.description: Slimy, dark spots or a sour smell. Avoid.

name: Green Peas
shortDescription: Fresh peas lose sweetness quickly once picked.
storageMethod: Keep peas in their pods in a bag in the refrigerator and shell them just before cooking. Freeze shelled peas after a quick blanch if you cannot use them soon.

shelfLife.refrigerator: In the pod: about 3–5 days. Shelled: about 2 days
shelfLife.freezer: Blanched: about 10–12 months

storageTips: Their sugar turns to starch over time, so cook them soon.
Plump, bright pods hold the sweetest peas.
Frozen peas are a good, long-lasting alternative.

freshnessStages.label: Fresh
freshnessStages.description: Bright green, plump, crisp pods.

freshnessStages.label: Use Soon
freshnessStages.description: Pods dulling or yellowing. Peas getting starchy.

freshnessStages.label: Check Quality
freshnessStages.description: Slimy pods, mould or a sour smell. Avoid.

name: Sweet Corn
shortDescription: Tastes sweetest on the day it is bought.
storageMethod: Keep corn in its husk in the refrigerator and cook it within a day or two. Its sugars turn to starch quickly, so the sooner the better.

shelfLife.refrigerator: In the husk: about 1–3 days
shelfLife.freezer: Blanched kernels: about 8–12 months

storageTips: Leave the husk on until cooking.
Moist, light-coloured silk means fresher corn.
Cut kernels off older cobs and use them in soups.

freshnessStages.label: Fresh
freshnessStages.description: Green husk, plump kernels that spurt juice when pressed.

freshnessStages.label: Use Soon
freshnessStages.description: Drying husk and silk, kernels less juicy.

freshnessStages.label: Check Quality
freshnessStages.description: Mould on the kernels or a sour smell. Avoid.

spoilageSigns: Mould on the kernels or under the husk

name: Coriander
shortDescription: Fresh dhania wilts within days unless it is kept cool and slightly damp.
storageMethod: Trim the stems and stand the bunch in a glass of water in the refrigerator with a bag loosely over the leaves, or wrap it in a barely damp paper towel inside a container.

shelfLife.refrigerator: About 1 week, stems in water or wrapped in damp paper
shelfLife.freezer: Chopped, in ice-cube trays with water or oil: about 6 months (for cooking)

storageTips: Remove rubber bands and yellow leaves before storing.
Wash only before using, then dry it well.
Blend wilting coriander into green chutney.

freshnessStages.label: Fresh
freshnessStages.description: Bright green, perky leaves, strong aroma.

freshnessStages.label: Use Soon
freshnessStages.description: Leaves wilting or a few turning yellow.

freshnessStages.label: Check Quality
freshnessStages.description: Slimy, black or mouldy leaves. Throw them out.

name: Mint
shortDescription: Pudina keeps best like a bunch of flowers: stems in water.
storageMethod: Stand the stems in a glass of water in the refrigerator with a bag loosely over the top, or wrap the bunch in a barely damp paper towel inside a container.

shelfLife.refrigerator: About 1 week
shelfLife.freezer: Chopped in ice-cube trays: about 6 months (for drinks and cooking)

storageTips: Pick off dark or slimy leaves before storing.
Dry the leaves after washing; wet mint blackens.
Dry extra mint in the shade and keep it in a jar.

freshnessStages.label: Fresh
freshnessStages.description: Bright green, firm leaves, strong cool smell.

freshnessStages.label: Use Soon
freshnessStages.description: Leaves softening or a few dark spots.

freshnessStages.label: Check Quality
freshnessStages.description: Black, slimy or mouldy leaves. Throw them out.

name: Zucchini
shortDescription: A mild summer squash that stays firm for about a week in the fridge.
storageMethod: Keep zucchini whole, dry and unwashed in the refrigerator crisper, loosely wrapped or in a paper bag. Wash it and trim the ends just before cooking.

shelfLife.refrigerator: About 4–7 days, whole and dry
shelfLife.freezer: Sliced and blanched: about 10–12 months (for cooking only)

storageTips: Moisture makes zucchini slimy, so store it dry.
Smaller zucchini are more tender and keep their texture better.
Grate a softening zucchini into batters, soups or sabzi.

freshnessStages.label: Fresh
freshnessStages.description: Firm, glossy skin and heavy for its size.

freshnessStages.label: Use Soon
freshnessStages.description: Slightly bendy or dull. Cook it in the next day or two.

freshnessStages.label: Check Quality
freshnessStages.description: Soft, slimy or mouldy spots. Avoid if in doubt.

name: Paneer
shortDescription: Fresh cheese with a short life; keep it cold, covered and moist.
storageMethod: Keep paneer in the refrigerator in a sealed container. Fresh paneer can be kept submerged in water that you change every day. Packaged paneer follows its label until opened.

shelfLife.refrigerator: Fresh or opened: about 2–3 days. Unopened packet: use by the label date
shelfLife.freezer: Cubed: about 2–3 months (slightly crumbly once thawed)

storageTips: Soak refrigerated paneer in warm water for a few minutes to soften it before cooking.
Use a clean knife and container to avoid contamination.
Do not leave paneer out at room temperature for more than about 2 hours.

freshnessStages.label: Fresh
freshnessStages.description: White, soft, mild milky smell.

freshnessStages.label: Use Soon
freshnessStages.description: Edges drying or slightly yellow. Cook it in a curry today.

freshnessStages.label: Check Quality
freshnessStages.description: Slimy surface, sour smell or mould. Throw it out.

name: Butter
shortDescription: Keeps for weeks in the fridge; light and air make it taste stale.
storageMethod: Keep butter wrapped or in a covered dish in the refrigerator, away from strong-smelling foods. Keep only a small amount out for spreading and use it within a day or two.

shelfLife.roomTemperature: A small portion in a covered dish: about 1–2 days
shelfLife.refrigerator: About 1–3 months; check the label date
shelfLife.freezer: About 6–9 months, well wrapped

storageTips: Butter absorbs fridge smells; keep it wrapped.
A darker yellow surface layer is oxidised; scrape it off.
Salted butter keeps a little longer than unsalted.

freshnessStages.label: Fresh
freshnessStages.description: Even pale yellow, sweet, creamy smell.

freshnessStages.label: Use Soon
freshnessStages.description: Darker yellow edges or picking up fridge smells.

freshnessStages.label: Check Quality
freshnessStages.description: Sour, cheesy or rancid smell, or mould. Avoid.

name: Ghee
shortDescription: Clarified butter with almost no water, so it keeps for months.
storageMethod: Keep ghee in a clean, tightly closed glass or steel jar in a cool, dark cupboard. Always use a dry spoon; water or food crumbs shorten its life.

shelfLife.pantry: Opened: about 3 months in a cool, dark place. Unopened: check the label
shelfLife.refrigerator: Opened: up to about 1 year (it becomes firm)

storageTips: Never put a wet or used spoon in the jar.
Keep the jar away from the stove's heat.
Ghee can be grainy or smooth; both are normal.

freshnessStages.label: Fresh
freshnessStages.description: Golden, nutty smell, smooth or grainy texture.

freshnessStages.label: Use Soon
freshnessStages.description: Smell getting flat; nearing the label date.

freshnessStages.label: Check Quality
freshnessStages.description: Sour, rancid smell or mould. Throw it out.

spoilageSigns: Very dark colour or bitter taste

name: Wheat Flour
shortDescription: Whole-wheat atta contains oils that slowly turn stale.
storageMethod: Keep atta in a clean, dry, airtight container in a cool pantry. For long storage, keep it in the refrigerator or freezer to slow staleness and keep insects out.

shelfLife.pantry: Whole-wheat atta: about 1–3 months. Refined flour (maida): about 6–8 months
shelfLife.refrigerator: Whole-wheat atta: about 6 months
shelfLife.freezer: About 1 year

storageTips: Do not mix new flour on top of old; finish the old batch first.
Keep the container away from the sink and stove steam.
A bay leaf in the container is a traditional insect deterrent.

freshnessStages.label: Fresh
freshnessStages.description: Dry, loose, neutral or slightly sweet smell.

freshnessStages.label: Use Soon
freshnessStages.description: Nearing three months open, or a faint stale smell.

freshnessStages.label: Check Quality
freshnessStages.description: Bitter or musty smell, insects, lumps or mould. Avoid.

name: Lentils
shortDescription: Dry dal keeps for a long time; cooked dal needs the fridge.
storageMethod: Store dry lentils in an airtight container in a cool, dry pantry. Refrigerate cooked dal within about 2 hours and reheat it until it is steaming hot.

shelfLife.pantry: Dry: about 1 year for best quality
shelfLife.refrigerator: Cooked dal: about 3–4 days in a sealed container
shelfLife.freezer: Cooked dal: about 2–3 months

storageTips: Older lentils take longer to cook but are still fine.
Check for small insects before washing.
Cool cooked dal quickly in a shallow container before refrigerating.

freshnessStages.label: Dry: Stable
freshnessStages.description: Dry, loose, even colour.

freshnessStages.label: Cooked: Fresh
freshnessStages.description: Just cooked and refrigerated within 2 hours.

freshnessStages.label: Cooked: Use Soon
freshnessStages.description: Third or fourth day in the fridge. Reheat well.

freshnessStages.label: Check Quality
freshnessStages.description: Sour smell, froth or mould in cooked dal. Throw it out.

spoilageSigns: Insects or webbing in dry lentils
Sour smell or bubbles in cooked dal
